claim: PhIP-seq allows for unbiased, proteome-wide autoantibody discovery across a variety of disease settings.
source: Phage immunoprecipitation sequencing (PhIP-seq) allows for unbiased, proteome-wide autoantibody discovery across a variety of disease settings, with identification of disease-specific autoantigens providing new insight into previously poorly understood forms of immune dysregulation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a general capability of the PhIP-seq technique.

claim: Current PhIP-seq protocols are inherently difficult to scale to accommodate large cohorts of cases and healthy controls.
source: Despite several successful implementations of PhIP-seq for autoantigen discovery, including our previous work (Vazquez et al., 2020), current protocols are inherently difficult to scale to accommodate large cohorts of cases and importantly, healthy controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and represents a limitation that motivated the current study.

claim: Scaled PhIP-seq datasets enable machine-learning approaches that result in robust prediction of disease status.
source: We demonstrate that these scaled datasets enable machine-learning approaches that result in robust prediction of disease status, as well as the ability to detect both known and novel autoantigens, such as prodynorphin (PDYN) in APS1 patients, and intestinally expressed proteins BEST4 and BTNL8 in IPEX patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by the machine learning analysis presented in the manuscript showing AUC = 0.95 for APS1 classification.

claim: PDYN is a novel autoantigen in APS1 patients.
source: We demonstrate that these scaled datasets enable machine-learning approaches that result in robust prediction of disease status, as well as the ability to detect both known and novel autoantigens, such as prodynorphin (PDYN) in APS1 patients, and intestinally expressed proteins BEST4 and BTNL8 in IPEX patients.
evidence: This is supported by PhIP-seq data and orthogonal validation by RLBA shown in Figure 3C.

claim: BEST4 is a novel autoantigen in IPEX patients.
source: We demonstrate that these scaled datasets enable machine-learning approaches that result in robust prediction of disease status, as well as the ability to detect both known and novel autoantigens, such as prodynorphin (PDYN) in APS1 patients, and intestinally expressed proteins BEST4 and BTNL8 in IPEX patients.
evidence: This is supported by PhIP-seq data and orthogonal validation by RLBA shown in Figure 5B.

claim: BTNL8 is a novel autoantigen in IPEX patients.
source: We demonstrate that these scaled datasets enable machine-learning approaches that result in robust prediction of disease status, as well as the ability to detect both known and novel autoantigens, such as prodynorphin (PDYN) in APS1 patients, and intestinally expressed proteins BEST4 and BTNL8 in IPEX patients.
evidence: This is supported by PhIP-seq data and orthogonal validation by RLBA shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: BEST4 antibodies were found in two patients with RAG1/2 deficiency, one of whom had very early onset IBD.
source: Remarkably, BEST4 antibodies were also found in two patients with RAG1/2 deficiency, one of whom had very early onset IBD.
evidence: This is supported by PhIP-seq data and orthogonal validation shown in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: CGNL1 is a rare, overlapping antigen between MIS-C and KD.
source: Scaled PhIP-seq examination of both MIS-C and KD demonstrated rare, overlapping antigens, including CGNL1, as well as several strongly enriched putative pneumonia-associated antigens in severe COVID-19, including the endosomal protein EEA1.
evidence: This is supported by PhIP-seq data and orthogonal validation by RLBA shown in Figure 6D.

claim: EEA1 is a putative pneumonia-associated antigen in severe COVID-19.
source: Scaled PhIP-seq examination of both MIS-C and KD demonstrated rare, overlapping antigens, including CGNL1, as well as several strongly enriched putative pneumonia-associated antigens in severe COVID-19, including the endosomal protein EEA1.
evidence: This is supported by PhIP-seq data showing enrichment in >10% of severe COVID-19 patients shown in Figure 7A.

claim: PhIP-seq was originally developed by Larman et al., 2011.
source: On the other hand, PhIP-seq, originally developed by Larman et al., 2011, uses the economy of scale of arrayed oligonucleotide synthesis to enable very large libraries at comparatively low cost.
evidence: This is a citation to the original development of the technique.

claim: PhIP-seq libraries express programmed sets of linear peptides and are inherently less sensitive to detect reactivity to conformational antigens.
source: From a technical standpoint, PhIP-seq libraries express programmed sets of linear peptides, and thus this technique is inherently less sensitive to detect reactivity to conformational antigens, such as Type I interferons (IFNs) and GAD65 (Vazquez et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work demonstrating this limitation.

claim: Many forms of autoimmunity exhibit significant phenotypic heterogeneity.
source: Given that many forms of autoimmunity exhibit significant phenotypic heterogeneity, the true number of patients with shared disease-associated autoantibodies may be low (Ferre et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The scaled PhIP-seq protocol allows 600-800 samples to be run in parallel.
source: Here, we develop a high-throughput PhIP-seq protocol with markedly increased accessibility (not requiring robotics) and scale (enabling 600–800 samples to be run in parallel), with minimal plate-to-plate variability and low contamination potential, and without sacrificing data quality.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the capabilities of the developed protocol.

claim: The scaled PhIP-seq protocol does not require robotics.
source: Here, we develop a high-throughput PhIP-seq protocol with markedly increased accessibility (not requiring robotics) and scale (enabling 600–800 samples to be run in parallel), with minimal plate-to-plate variability and low contamination potential, and without sacrificing data quality.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the accessibility of the developed protocol.

claim: The vacuum-based protocol data is closely correlated with moderate-throughput manual multichannel protocol data for APS1 samples.
source: The data for APS1 samples on our moderate-throughput manual multichannel protocols were closely correlated with vacuum-based output, including identification of previously validated antigens within each sample (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Each APS1 patient is known to have multiple, high-affinity antibodies to self-proteins.
source: As each APS1 patient is known to have multiple, high-affinity antibodies to self-proteins (Fishman et al., 2017; Landegren et al., 2016; Meyer et al., 2016; Vazquez et al., 2020) we reasoned that this would be an ideal cohort to determine whether a global autoreactive state was discernible.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Each individual sample exhibits a spectrum of enriched genes, regardless of disease status.
source: As expected, each individual sample exhibits a spectrum of enriched genes, regardless of disease status (Figure 2A), indicating that measures of simple enrichment are inadequate for discrimination of cases from controls.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Measures of simple enrichment are inadequate for discrimination of cases from controls.
source: As expected, each individual sample exhibits a spectrum of enriched genes, regardless of disease status (Figure 2A), indicating that measures of simple enrichment are inadequate for discrimination of cases from controls.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Increasing the number of healthy control samples from 10 to 50 removes 388 non-specific hits.
source: Using these conservative criteria, a control set of 10 samples resulted in (on average) 404 apparent hits, while increasing the control set to 50 samples removed an additional 388 non-specific hits, leaving 16 apparent hits (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the downsampling analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Further increasing the number of control samples to 150 samples removes 4-5 more autoantigen candidates.
source: Further increasing the number of control samples to 150 samples had diminishing returns, although 4–5 more autoantigen candidates were removed as being non-specific, reducing the frequency of false positives, and ultimately leaving only ~1% of the original candidate list for further investigation.
evidence: This is supported by the downsampling analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: PhIP-seq experimental design should include a large and appropriate number of non-disease controls to improve downstream analysis.
source: In sum, to improve downstream analysis aimed at detecting disease-associated hits, PhIP-seq experimental design should include a large and appropriate number of non-disease controls.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the control cohort size analysis.

claim: All hits present in at least 10% of APS1 patients spanned all three cohorts (two North American and one Swedish).
source: All hits present in at least 10% of APS1 patients also spanned all three cohorts, thus further validating broad prevalence of antigens that were previously described by us (RFX6, ACPT, TRIM50, CROCC2, GIP, NKX6-3, KHDC3L) and others (SOX10, LCN1) (Figure 2C; Fishman et al., 2017; Hedstrand et al., 2001; Vazquez et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2C and citations to previous work.

claim: 39 candidate hits were detected that were present in >4% of APS1 patients and in 2 or fewer controls.
source: At the gene level, we detected 39 candidate hits that were present in 6/128 (>4%) of APS1 and in 2 or fewer controls (2/186, 1%) (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: PDYN was enriched by 4.7% of APS1 patient samples.
source: PDYN was enriched by 6/128 (4.7%) of patient samples and subsequently was validated by Radioligand Binding Assay (RLBA) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the PhIP-seq data and validation shown in Figure 3C.

claim: PDYN is a secreted opioid peptide thought to be involved in regulation of addiction-related behaviors.
source: For example, PDYN is a secreted opioid peptide thought to be involved in regulation of addiction-related behaviors (reviewed in Fricker et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: SPAG17 is closely related to the known APS1 autoantigen SPAG16.
source: For example, SPAG17 is closely related to the known APS1 autoantigen SPAG16 and is expressed primarily in male germ cells and in the lung, with murine genetic mutations resulting in ciliary dyskinesis with pulmonary phenotypes (Fishman et al., 2017; Teves et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SPAG17 is expressed primarily in male germ cells and in the lung.
source: For example, SPAG17 is closely related to the known APS1 autoantigen SPAG16 and is expressed primarily in male germ cells and in the lung, with murine genetic mutations resulting in ciliary dyskinesis with pulmonary phenotypes (Fishman et al., 2017; Teves et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Murine genetic mutations in SPAG17 result in ciliary dyskinesis with pulmonary phenotypes.
source: For example, SPAG17 is closely related to the known APS1 autoantigen SPAG16 and is expressed primarily in male germ cells and in the lung, with murine genetic mutations resulting in ciliary dyskinesis with pulmonary phenotypes (Fishman et al., 2017; Teves et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: CROCC2/Rootletin is a protein expressed in ciliated cells.
source: Also potentially related to ciliary and/or pulmonary autoimmunity is CROCC2/Rootletin, a protein expressed in ciliated cells, which we previously observed, and now recognize at a high frequency across multiple cohorts (Uhlén et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: GAS2L2 is a ciliary protein expressed in the airway.
source: Similarly, GAS2L2 is a ciliary protein expressed in the airway, with genetic loss of function in mice resulting in impaired mucociliary clearance, and clustered closely with CROCC2 (Bustamante-Marin et al., 2019; Uhlén et al., 2015) in this dataset.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Genetic loss of function of GAS2L2 in mice results in impaired mucociliary clearance.
source: Similarly, GAS2L2 is a ciliary protein expressed in the airway, with genetic loss of function in mice resulting in impaired mucociliary clearance, and clustered closely with CROCC2 (Bustamante-Marin et al., 2019; Uhlén et al., 2015) in this dataset.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: CT45A10 and GPR64 are both proteins with expression restricted primarily to male gonadal tissues.
source: CT45A10 and GPR64 are both proteins with expression restricted primarily to male gonadal tissues (Uhlén et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: GABRR1 is a GABA receptor expressed primarily in the central nervous system as well as on platelets.
source: GABRR1 is a GABA receptor expressed primarily in the central nervous system as well as on platelets (Ge et al., 2006; Zhu et al., 2019), and TRIM2 is implicated in genetic disorders of demyelination within the peripheral nervous system, and therefore may be of interest to the chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy phenotype that can be seen in some patients with APS1 (Li et al., 2020; Valenzise et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: TRIM2 is implicated in genetic disorders of demyelination within the peripheral nervous system.
source: GABRR1 is a GABA receptor expressed primarily in the central nervous system as well as on platelets (Ge et al., 2006; Zhu et al., 2019), and TRIM2 is implicated in genetic disorders of demyelination within the peripheral nervous system, and therefore may be of interest to the chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy phenotype that can be seen in some patients with APS1 (Li et al., 2020; Valenzise et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy can be seen in some patients with APS1.
source: GABRR1 is a GABA receptor expressed primarily in the central nervous system as well as on platelets (Ge et al., 2006; Zhu et al., 2019), and TRIM2 is implicated in genetic disorders of demyelination within the peripheral nervous system, and therefore may be of interest to the chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy phenotype that can be seen in some patients with APS1 (Li et al., 2020; Valenzise et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: CDHR5 is a transmembrane cadherin-family protein expressed on the enterocyte cell surface.
source: In addition to our previously described intestinally expressed autoantigens RFX6, NKX6-3, and GIP, we also identify CDHR5, a transmembrane cadherin-family protein expressed on the enterocyte cell surface, as a putative autoantigen in APS1 (Crawley et al., 2014; Uhlén et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A logistic regression classifier applied to APS1 and control datasets resulted in excellent prediction of disease status with AUC = 0.95.
source: We applied a simple logistic regression classifier to our full gene-level APS1 (n=128) and control (n=186) datasets, resulting in excellent prediction of disease status (AUC = 0.95, Figure 4A) using fivefold cross-validation.
evidence: This is supported by the machine learning analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The classification model was driven strongly by many of the previously identified autoantigens, including RFX6 and KHDC3L.
source: Moreover, we found that the classification model was driven strongly by many of the previously identified autoantigens, including RFX6, KHDC3L, and others (Figure 4A), in addition to some targets that had not been previously examined (Vazquez et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the logistic regression coefficients shown in Figure 4B.

claim: IPEX syndrome is characterized by defective peripheral immune tolerance secondary to impaired T regulatory cell function.
source: IPEX syndrome is characterized by defective peripheral immune tolerance secondary to impaired T regulatory cell (Treg) function.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IPEX syndrome.

claim: In IPEX, peripheral tolerance rather than central tolerance is impaired.
source: In IPEX, peripheral tolerance rather than central tolerance is impaired, resulting in a phenotypic constellation of autoimmunity that partially overlaps with APS1 (Bacchetta et al., 2006; Powell et al., 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The majority of IPEX patients exhibit severe enteropathy with early-onset severe diarrhea and failure to thrive.
source: Notably, the majority of IPEX patients exhibit severe enteropathy, with early-onset severe diarrhea and failure to thrive, with many of these children harboring anti-enterocyte antibodies detected by indirect immunofluorescence (Bacchetta et al., 2006; Gambineri et al., 2018; Powell et al., 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Many IPEX patients harbor anti-enterocyte antibodies detected by indirect immunofluorescence.
source: Notably, the majority of IPEX patients exhibit severe enteropathy, with early-onset severe diarrhea and failure to thrive, with many of these children harboring anti-enterocyte antibodies detected by indirect immunofluorescence (Bacchetta et al., 2006; Gambineri et al., 2018; Powell et al., 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Harmonin (USH1C) and ANKS4B are previously described IPEX autoantibodies.
source: A handful of IPEX autoantibodies targeting antigens expressed in the intestine have been described, including harmonin (USH1C) and ANKS4B (Eriksson et al., 2019; Kobayashi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Enrichment of USH1C was observed in two IPEX patients and was fully correlated with anti-ANKS5B.
source: In our data, enrichment of USH1C was observed in two IPEX patients, and this signal was fully correlated with anti-ANKS5B as previously described (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Eriksson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and citation to previous work.

claim: BEST4 is a protein expressed by a specific subset of enterocytes.
source: Among these were several with expression restricted to the intestine, including BEST4, a protein expressed by a specific subset of enterocytes, BTNL8, a butyrophilin-like molecule highly expressed in the gut epithelium, ST6GALNAC1, and ITGA4 (Figure 5A; Mayassi et al., 2019; Schaum et al., 2018; Uhlén et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: BTNL8 is a butyrophilin-like molecule highly expressed in the gut epithelium.
source: Among these were several with expression restricted to the intestine, including BEST4, a protein expressed by a specific subset of enterocytes, BTNL8, a butyrophilin-like molecule highly expressed in the gut epithelium, ST6GALNAC1, and ITGA4 (Figure 5A; Mayassi et al., 2019; Schaum et al., 2018; Uhlén et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: 4/26 (15%) of IPEX patients were positive for anti-BEST4 autoantibodies.
source: A total of 4/26 (15%) of IPEX patients were positive for anti-BEST4 autoantibodies (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the validation data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: 11/26 (42%) of IPEX patients were positive for anti-BTNL8 antibodies.
source: In the case of BTLN8, orthogonal validation identified 11/26 (42%) of IPEX patients who were positive for anti-BTNL8 antibodies (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the validation data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: All IPEX patients with anti-BTNL8 and/or BEST4 antibodies had clinical evidence of enteropathy.
source: Of note, all patients with anti-BTNL8 and/or BEST4 antibodies also had clinical evidence of enteropathy (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by clinical data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: 3/15 (20%) patients in a second, independent IPEX cohort were positive for anti-BTNL8 antibodies.
source: In addition, to broaden the validity of our findings, we tested a second, independent cohort of IPEX patients for anti-BTNL8 antibodies and found 3/15 (20%) patients to be positive (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by the validation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Anti-BEST4 and anti-BTNL8 are associated with IPEX enteropathy.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that anti-BEST4 and anti-BTNL8 are associated with IPEX enteropathy.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the validation data and clinical correlations.

claim: Hypomorphic RAG1/2 mutations represent a phenotypically heterogeneous form of monogenic immune dysregulation.
source: Hypomorphic RAG1/2 mutations represent an additional and notoriously phenotypically heterogeneous form of monogenic immune dysregulation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RAG1/2 deficiency.

claim: Absent RAG complex activity leads to lack of peripheral T and B cells, causing severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID).
source: Absent RAG complex activity leads to lack of peripheral T and B cells, therefore causing severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID).
evidence: This is established knowledge about RAG complex function.

claim: Patients with hypomorphic RAG1/2 have residual capacity to generate T and B cells.
source: However, patients with hypomorphic RAG1/2 have residual capacity to generate T and B cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about hypomorphic RAG1/2 mutations.

claim: Patients with hypomorphic RAG1/2 can present with Omenn syndrome, atypical SCID (AS), or combined immune deficiency with granulomas and autoimmunity (CID-G/AI).
source: Depending on the severity of the defect, these patients can present with Omenn syndrome, atypical SCID (AS), or combined immune deficiency with granulomas and autoimmunity (CID-G/AI) (Delmonte et al., 2018; Delmonte et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Autoimmune manifestations are particularly common in patients with AS and CID-G/AI.
source: Autoimmune manifestations are particularly common in patients with AS and CID-G/AI.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RAG1/2 deficiency phenotypes.

claim: Cytopenias are the most frequent form of autoimmunity in patients with RAG deficiency.
source: Cytopenias are the most frequent form of autoimmunity in patients with RAG deficiency, but cutaneous, neuromuscular, and intestinal manifestations have been also reported.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RAG deficiency.

claim: Anti-cytokine antibodies have been described in RAG deficiency.
source: While anti-cytokine antibodies have been described, other disease-associated autoantibody targets remain to be identified (Delmonte et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Two RAG1/2 patients with anti-BEST4 antibodies both had CID-G/AI.
source: Both positive patients had CID-G/AI, indicating the presence of autoimmune features.
evidence: This is clinical information about the patients with anti-BEST4 antibodies.

claim: One of the two RAG1/2 patients with anti-BEST4 antibodies had very early-onset inflammatory bowel disease.
source: Remarkably – given that enteropathy in the setting of hypomorphic RAG1/2 deficiency is rare – one of the two individuals harboring anti-BEST4 antibodies also had very early-onset inflammatory bowel disease.
evidence: This is clinical information about one of the patients with anti-BEST4 antibodies.

claim: Nearly half of the RAG1/2 deficiency cohort sera were enriched for peptides derived from ZNF365.
source: Nearly half of the cohort sera were enriched for peptides derived from ZNF365 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Variants in ZNF365 are associated with Crohn's disease and autoimmune uveitis.
source: ZNF365 is a protein associated with multiple autoimmune diseases, as evidenced by genome-wide association studies (GWAS) show that variants in ZNF365 are associated with Crohn's disease and autoimmune uveitis (Haritunians et al., 2011; Hou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to GWAS studies.

claim: RELL2 is a TNF receptor binding partner.
source: Many patients also had evidence of autoantibodies targeting RELL2, a TNF receptor binding partner, and CEACAM3, a phagocyte receptor that recognizes human-specific pathogens and is important for opsonin-independent phagocytosis of bacteria (Bonsignore et al., 2019; Moua et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: CEACAM3 is a phagocyte receptor that recognizes human-specific pathogens and is important for opsonin-independent phagocytosis of bacteria.
source: Many patients also had evidence of autoantibodies targeting RELL2, a TNF receptor binding partner, and CEACAM3, a phagocyte receptor that recognizes human-specific pathogens and is important for opsonin-independent phagocytosis of bacteria (Bonsignore et al., 2019; Moua et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: MIS-C leads to critical illness in ~70% of affected children.
source: MIS-C leads to critical illness in ~70% of affected children and shares some common clinical features with KD, the most common cause of acquired pediatric heart disease in the United States.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about MIS-C.

claim: KD is the most common cause of acquired pediatric heart disease in the United States.
source: MIS-C leads to critical illness in ~70% of affected children and shares some common clinical features with KD, the most common cause of acquired pediatric heart disease in the United States.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about KD.

claim: The etiologies of both KD and MIS-C remain enigmatic.
source: Despite hints for a role of abnormal adaptive immunity and autoantibodies in the pathogenesis of KD and MIS-C, the etiologies of both diseases remain enigmatic (Feldstein et al., 2020; Newburger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A previous PhIP-seq study of MIS-C included only four healthy controls and nine MIS-C patients.
source: However, this study included only four healthy controls and nine MIS-C patients, and as our results have shown, removal of false-positive PhIP-seq hits requires the use of substantial numbers of unaffected controls (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a citation to previous work (Gruber et al., 2020) and a critique based on the current study's findings.

claim: No evidence for specific enrichment was observed for any of the previously reported MIS-C candidate antigens that overlapped with the PhIP-seq library.
source: No evidence for specific enrichment was observed for any of the previously reported candidate antigens that overlapped with our PhIP-seq library (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: MIS-C patients are treated with IVIG, which has abundant low-affinity, low-avidity autoantibodies.
source: Additionally, MIS-C patients are treated with IVIG, which has abundant low-affinity, low-avidity autoantibodies, so caution must be exercised in the timing of sample collection (Burbelo et al., 2021; Sacco et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The majority of MIS-C samples are confirmed to be collected pre-IVIG.
source: While it remains unclear whether high-affinity, novel autoantibodies are likely to be present in IVIG, the majority of our MIS-C samples are confirmed to be collected pre-IVIG.
evidence: This is information about the sample collection timing.

claim: Analysis of the MIS-C cohort yielded only three candidate hits: CD34, RPS6KB1, and CAPZB, each in 2/20 patient sera.
source: Analysis of our MIS-C cohort for shared candidate hits yielded only three candidate hits, each in 2/20 patient sera. These were CD34, RPS6KB1, and CAPZB (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A much larger MIS-C cohort will be required to detect rare, shared antigens with confidence by PhIP-seq.
source: These results suggest that a much larger MIS-C cohort, controlled by an equally large set of healthy controls, will be required to detect rare, shared antigens with confidence by PhIP-seq.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the limited findings in the MIS-C cohort.

claim: 25 shared hits were detected among 3 or more of the 70 KD samples, which were specific to KD relative to adult healthy controls.
source: Using the same hit selection criteria as previously, we detected 25 shared hits among 3 or more of the 70 KD samples, which were specific to KD relative to adult healthy controls (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: 17 of the 25 shared KD hits were absent from febrile pediatric patients.
source: Of these 25 shared KD hits, 17 were absent from additional control groups including the febrile pediatric patients.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis comparing KD to febrile controls.

claim: Each of the KD candidate antigens was present in only a small subset of KD samples, suggesting significant heterogeneity.
source: Each of these hits was present in only a small subset of KD samples, suggesting significant heterogeneity among samples.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing low frequency of each hit.

claim: SPATA2 is a protein known to regulate the TNF receptor response.
source: Some of the candidate antigens have possible connections to the systemic inflammation seen in KD, including SPATA2 (6/70, 8.6%) and ALOX5B (4/70, 5.7%). SPATA2 is a protein known to regulate the TNF receptor response, with murine knockout of SPATA2 resulting in increased activation of NFkB and MAPK (Schlicher and Maurer, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Murine knockout of SPATA2 results in increased activation of NFkB and MAPK.
source: SPATA2 is a protein known to regulate the TNF receptor response, with murine knockout of SPATA2 resulting in increased activation of NFkB and MAPK (Schlicher and Maurer, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: ALOX15 family of lipoxygenases is responsive to Th2-induced anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-4 and IL-13 in human macrophages.
source: Similarly, ALOX15 family of lipoxygenases is known to be responsive to Th2-induced anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-4 and IL-13 in human macrophages and thereby likely plays a role in suppressing inflammatory responses, and polymorphisms have been linked to the development of coronary artery disease (Snodgrass and Brüne, 2019; Wuest et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: ALOX15 polymorphisms have been linked to the development of coronary artery disease.
source: Similarly, ALOX15 family of lipoxygenases is known to be responsive to Th2-induced anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-4 and IL-13 in human macrophages and thereby likely plays a role in suppressing inflammatory responses, and polymorphisms have been linked to the development of coronary artery disease (Snodgrass and Brüne, 2019; Wuest et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Pancreatitis and psoriasis have been reported as rare complications of KD.
source: For example, pancreatitis and psoriasis have been reported as rare complications of KD (Asano et al., 2005; Haddock et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: 7/70 (10%) of KD patients have increased signal for autoantibodies targeting FBXL19.
source: We found that 7/70 of the KD patients (10%) have increased signal for autoantibodies targeting FBXL19, a protein with associations with both acute pancreatitis (Ma et al., 2020) and psoriasis (Stuart et al., 2010) and 10/70 for pancreas-expressed protein RESP18 (Zhang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the PhIP-seq data.

claim: FBXL19 is a protein with associations with both acute pancreatitis and psoriasis.
source: We found that 7/70 of the KD patients (10%) have increased signal for autoantibodies targeting FBXL19, a protein with associations with both acute pancreatitis (Ma et al., 2020) and psoriasis (Stuart et al., 2010) and 10/70 for pancreas-expressed protein RESP18 (Zhang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: 6 of the 17 KD-specific hits were present in one or more MIS-C samples.
source: Given the partial clinical overlap of KD with MIS-C, we also searched for the low-frequency, shared KD hits within MIS-C and found that 6 of the 17 KD hits were present in one or more MIS-C samples (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: CGNL1 is an endothelial junction protein highly expressed in the cardiac endothelium.
source: CGNL1 is an endothelial junction protein and is highly expressed in the cardiac endothelium (Chrifi et al., 2017; Schaum et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Anti-CGNL1 autoantibodies were confirmed using a radioligand binding assay with whole CGNL1 protein.
source: We confirmed anti-CGNL1 autoantibodies using a radioligand binding assay with whole CGNL1 protein (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by the validation data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Over 10% of severe COVID-19 pneumonia is characterized by the presence of anti-Type I IFN autoantibodies.
source: Recently, it was reported that over 10% of severe COVID-19 pneumonia is characterized by the presence of anti-Type I IFN autoantibodies, a specificity that overlaps with APS1 (Bastard et al., 2020; Bastard et al., 2021b; Bastard et al., 2021a; Meager et al., 2006; Meyer et al., 2016; van der Wijst et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Low sensitivity for anti-type I IFN autoantibodies by PhIP-seq is likely due to the conformational nature of these antigens.
source: As expected, we had low sensitivity for the known anti-type I IFN autoantibodies by PhIP-seq, likely due to the conformational nature of these antigens; however, this cohort had been previously assessed for anti-Type I IFN antibodies by other techniques (Bastard et al., 2020; Bastard et al., 2021c).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known limitations of PhIP-seq for conformational antigens.

claim: No substantial overlap was detected between APS1 antigens and severe COVID-19 antigens beyond anti-Type I IFN.
source: We did not detect substantial overlap of any of the other antigens that were found in 5% or more of APS1 samples, suggesting that autoantibody commonalities between APS1 and severe COVID-19 may be limited (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: EEA1 is an early endosomal protein.
source: A small number of putative autoantigens were identified in four or more of the severe COVID-19 group (>4%), but not within our control group, including MCAM, CHRM5, and EEA1. Of these, only EEA1, an early endosomal protein, had a frequency of >10% (Mu et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: EEA1 had a frequency of >10% in severe COVID-19 patients.
source: Of these, only EEA1, an early endosomal protein, had a frequency of >10% (Mu et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by the PhIP-seq data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The set of anti-EEA1 positive patients was almost fully distinct from the anti-Type I IFN antibody positive group.
source: Notably, the set of anti-EEA1 positive patients was almost fully distinct from the anti-Type I IFN antibody positive group, with only one patient shared between the groups (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Anti-EEA1 antibodies may have predictive potential worth further investigation in COVID-19.
source: Given the importance of the finding of autoantibodies to Type 1 IFNs in >15% of critical COVID-19 pneumonia, our data suggest that anti-EEA1 antibodies may also have predictive potential worth further investigation.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the data.

claim: Declining costs in sequencing paired with scaled protocols result in low per-sample cost and experimental time.
source: Continually declining costs in sequencing paired with scaled protocols such as the ones presented here result in a low per-sample cost and experimental time, and declining costs of custom oligonucleotide based-libraries allow for extensive adaptation (Román-Meléndez et al., 2021; Vogl et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a general statement about the economics of the technique.

claim: The scaled data reinforces the importance of including large control cohorts to improve specificity.
source: Our scaled data reinforces the importance of including large control cohorts to improve specificity and orthogonal validations to evaluate sensitivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the control cohort size analysis.

claim: Orthogonal validations are important to evaluate sensitivity of PhIP-seq.
source: Our scaled data reinforces the importance of including large control cohorts to improve specificity and orthogonal validations to evaluate sensitivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the validation experiments.

claim: The absence of appropriately sized control cohorts can result in false-positive associations between enriched protein sequences and disease.
source: The absence of appropriately sized control cohorts can result in false-positive associations between enriched protein sequences and disease which can lead to misinterpretation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the control cohort size analysis.

claim: PhIP-seq is optimized for linear antigens and is inherently less robust for detection of conformational or modified epitopes.
source: Furthermore, PhIP-seq is optimized for linear antigens and thus is inherently less robust for detection of confirmational or modified epitopes.
evidence: This is a known limitation of the PhIP-seq technique.

claim: Known anti-IFN and anti-GAD65 antibodies can be detected only in a handful of APS1 samples by PhIP-seq, while orthogonal assays using whole conformation protein demonstrate increased sensitivity.
source: For example, our previous work highlights that known anti-IFN and anti-GAD65 antibodies can be detected only in a handful of APS1 samples by PhIP-seq, while orthogonal assays using whole conformation protein demonstrate increased sensitivity (Vazquez et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The increased sensitivity of whole protein validation relative to PhIP-seq for BTNL8 autoantibodies highlights the need for rapid and sensitive secondary assays.
source: Similarly, the increased sensitivity of whole protein validation relative to PhIP-seq for BTNL8 autoantibodies highlights the need for rapid and sensitive secondary assays to confirm or even increase the importance of a given candidate antigen.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the BTNL8 validation data.

claim: PDYN is a secreted opioid precursor of the central nervous system.
source: PDYN is a secreted opioid precursor of the central nervous system, and while PDYN-knockout mice are largely phenotypically normal, they do experience hyperalgesia and altered anxiety-related behaviors relative to wildtype mice (McLaughlin et al., 2003; Sharifi et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: PDYN-knockout mice experience hyperalgesia and altered anxiety-related behaviors relative to wildtype mice.
source: PDYN is a secreted opioid precursor of the central nervous system, and while PDYN-knockout mice are largely phenotypically normal, they do experience hyperalgesia and altered anxiety-related behaviors relative to wildtype mice (McLaughlin et al., 2003; Sharifi et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: BEST4 is a well-characterized, cell-surface intestinal ion channel.
source: BEST4 is a well-characterized, cell-surface intestinal ion channel (Qu and Hartzell, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: BEST4 has become a standard and specific marker for a subset of enterocytes in the duodenum and colon, including CFTR+ enterocytes.
source: Recently, BEST4 has become a standard and specific marker for a subset of enterocytes in the duodenum and colon, including CFTR+ enterocytes, which are involved in fluid homeostasis (Busslinger et al., 2021; Elmentaite et al., 2021; Smillie et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: CFTR+ enterocytes are involved in fluid homeostasis.
source: Recently, BEST4 has become a standard and specific marker for a subset of enterocytes in the duodenum and colon, including CFTR+ enterocytes, which are involved in fluid homeostasis (Busslinger et al., 2021; Elmentaite et al., 2021; Smillie et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The presence of BEST4 antigen within CID-G/AI suggests a possible etiologic link between IPEX and RAG deficiency, possibly relating to Treg dysfunction.
source: The presence of an IPEX antigen BEST4 within CID-G/AI suggests a possible etiologic link between the two diseases, possibly relating to Treg dysfunction.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the shared antigen finding.

claim: Future experiments searching for anti-BEST4 antibodies in IBD and other forms of autoimmune enteropathy are warranted.
source: Furthermore, given that BEST4 autoantibodies were found across two distinct etiologies of IBD, in addition to the intestinal localization of BEST4 expression, future experiments specifically searching for the presence of anti-BEST4 antibodies in IBD and other forms of autoimmune enteropathy are warranted.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings.

claim: BTN and BTNL-family members belong to the family of B7 co-stimulatory receptors known to modulate T-cell responses.
source: BTN and BTNL-family members belong to the family of B7 co-stimulatory receptors known to modulate T-cell responses, with structural similarity to CD80 and PD-L1 (Chapoval et al., 2013; Rhodes et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: BTNL-family members have structural similarity to CD80 and PD-L1.
source: BTN and BTNL-family members belong to the family of B7 co-stimulatory receptors known to modulate T-cell responses, with structural similarity to CD80 and PD-L1 (Chapoval et al., 2013; Rhodes et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: BTNL-family members are thought to participate primarily in regulation of gamma-delta T cells.
source: Broadly, BTNL-family members are thought to participate primarily in regulation of gamma-delta T cells, with BTNL8/BTNL3 implicated in gut epithelial immune homeostasis (Di Marco Barros et al., 2016; Chapoval et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: BTNL8/BTNL3 are implicated in gut epithelial immune homeostasis.
source: Broadly, BTNL-family members are thought to participate primarily in regulation of gamma-delta T cells, with BTNL8/BTNL3 implicated in gut epithelial immune homeostasis (Di Marco Barros et al., 2016; Chapoval et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Antibodies to BTNL8 could play a functional role in immune checkpoints rather than only a bystander role.
source: Given the cell-surface expression pattern of BTNL8, it is conceivable that antibodies to these proteins could play a functional role in immune checkpoints, rather than only the bystander role implicated for most autoantibodies to intracellular antigens.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the known biology of BTNL8.

claim: Recent studies in celiac disease patients demonstrated a reduction in BTNL3/BTNL8 expression following acute episodes of inflammation.
source: Interestingly, recent studies in patients with celiac disease have demonstrated a reduction in BTNL3/BTNL8 expression following acute episodes of inflammation, with an associated loss of the physiological normal gamma/delta T-cell subset of gut intraepithelial lymphocytes (Mayassi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Celiac disease patients show an associated loss of the physiological normal gamma/delta T-cell subset of gut intraepithelial lymphocytes following inflammation.
source: Interestingly, recent studies in patients with celiac disease have demonstrated a reduction in BTNL3/BTNL8 expression following acute episodes of inflammation, with an associated loss of the physiological normal gamma/delta T-cell subset of gut intraepithelial lymphocytes (Mayassi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Both KD and MIS-C respond to varying degrees to IVIG therapy.
source: Nonetheless, a number of observations point to a possible role for abnormal adaptive immunity and autoantibodies (reviewed in Sakurai, 2019). Both diseases respond to varying degrees to IVIG therapy, and genetic studies suggest some children with polymorphisms in genes involving B-cell and antibody function can be predisposed to developing KD (reviewed in Onouchi, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Genetic studies suggest some children with polymorphisms in genes involving B-cell and antibody function can be predisposed to developing KD.
source: Both diseases respond to varying degrees to IVIG therapy, and genetic studies suggest some children with polymorphisms in genes involving B-cell and antibody function can be predisposed to developing KD (reviewed in Onouchi, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Autoantibodies targeting clinically relevant tissues such as the heart or endothelium have been detected in KD.
source: Autoantibodies targeting clinically relevant tissues such as the heart or endothelium have been detected in KD, though their role in disease pathogenesis is uncertain (Cunningham et al., 1999; Fujieda et al., 1997; Grunebaum et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The role of autoantibodies in KD pathogenesis is uncertain.
source: Autoantibodies targeting clinically relevant tissues such as the heart or endothelium have been detected in KD, though their role in disease pathogenesis is uncertain (Cunningham et al., 1999; Fujieda et al., 1997; Grunebaum et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Anti-CGNL1 antibodies may represent a subset of specificities within anti-endothelial cell antibodies.
source: Although anti-CGNL1 antibodies were only found at low frequency, it is possible that these antibodies may represent a subset of specificities within anti-endothelial cell antibodies, given the endothelial expression of CGNL1 as well as its implications in cardiovascular disease (Chrifi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the known biology of CGNL1.

claim: CGNL1 has implications in cardiovascular disease.
source: Although anti-CGNL1 antibodies were only found at low frequency, it is possible that these antibodies may represent a subset of specificities within anti-endothelial cell antibodies, given the endothelial expression of CGNL1 as well as its implications in cardiovascular disease (Chrifi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Anti-EEA1 antibodies have previously been reported in systemic lupus erythematosus.
source: Interestingly, similarly to anti-IFN antibodies, anti-EEA1 antibodies have also previously been reported in the setting of systemic lupus erythematosus (Selak et al., 2000; Stinton et al., 2004; Waite et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: PhIP-seq data may have predictive or diagnostic value when cohorts are sufficiently large.
source: This work suggests that PhIP-seq data may have predictive or diagnostic value when the cohorts are sufficiently large.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the machine learning analysis.

claim: Machine learning techniques will be effective tools for determining the underlying proteins that drive successful classification using PhIP-seq data.
source: Thus, scaled PhIP-seq represents an avenue to not only discover and compare novel autoantigens within and across cohorts of autoimmune disease, but also suggests that machine learning techniques will be effective tools for determining, without supervision, the underlying proteins that drive successful classification using this data type.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the machine learning analysis.

claim: Full PhIP-seq data availability is critical for enabling expanded analysis and comparison across datasets, cohorts, and research groups.
source: Finally, we emphasize that to broadly understand autoantibody profiles, full PhIP-seq data availability is critical for enabling expanded analysis and comparison across datasets, cohorts, and research groups.
evidence: This is a recommendation for best practices in data sharing.

claim: Full PhIP-seq data for all cohorts will be available for download at Dryad.
source: Full PhIP-seq data for all cohorts presented here will be linked to this publication and will be available for download at Dryad.
evidence: This is a statement about data availability.
